kept.a:
Oysters Rockefeller is a New Orleans original, and this appetizer is the Thanksgiving Day kitchen’s gratin of it. The dish was created at Antoine’s in the French Quarter, around 1899 by most accounts, and is credited to Jules Alciatore, the founder’s son. It was named for John D. Rockefeller, the richest American of the day, for the richness of its green sauce. Antoine’s still keeps its recipe a secret and has long said it holds no spinach; most cooks since have used spinach.

Ours, on the sheet, is oysters, bacon, creamed spinach and breadcrumbs, baked as a gratin. Gratin comes from the French gratter, to scrape, and names the browned crust on top. Expect briny oysters, smoky bacon, creamy spinach and a crisp crumb.

The sheet prints no method: learn at lineup whether it is baked in the shell or in one dish, how many oysters come in a portion and where they are from.

Lead with the story: guests know oysters Rockefeller, and it was born in the French Quarter, like our own house. Offer this to the oyster lover and to anyone who wants a warm, rich start before the turkey. Say: “It’s our Thanksgiving take on oysters Rockefeller: oysters baked with bacon and creamed spinach under a crisp crumb.” Then offer a glass of our house Champagne, whose bubbles cut the cream and the bacon.

Asked: Is this oysters Rockefeller?

Answer: It is our Thanksgiving Day gratin of it. The classic from Antoine’s is oysters on the half shell baked under a rich green sauce; ours bakes oysters with bacon and creamed spinach under breadcrumbs.

Asked: Is there spinach in the original?

Answer: Antoine’s keeps its recipe secret and has long said there is none. Most versions since use spinach, and ours lists creamed spinach.

Asked: Are the oysters raw?

Answer: No, the gratin is baked and comes to the table hot. How the oysters are handled is the kitchen’s to say, so check at lineup before you promise more.

It is a Thanksgiving Day dish only: do not offer it on another night. The sheet prints no method, so do not say how the oysters are cooked or where they come from until the kitchen tells you. It is rich, so steer a guest who wants a light start to the salad or the crudo. A question about shellfish, pork or any diet goes to the kitchen before you answer. kept.a:
The Endive Satsuma Salad is the lightest of the six Thanksgiving Day appetizers, and the one that tastes of a south Louisiana fall.

Satsuma is a mandarin first recorded in Japan and named for the old Satsuma province. It is usually seedless and peels easily, and it is the main citrus of south Louisiana, where Plaquemines Parish is the leading grower; the harvest runs from about October into December. Endive is a leaf of the chicory family, pale, crisp and gently bitter. Belgian endive is grown in the dark from chicory roots, which keeps it white; the Flemish call it witloof, white leaf.

The sheet adds a cherry vinaigrette and roasted sunflower seeds: sweet and tart fruit against the bitter leaf, and crunch. Whether the endive is Belgian or curly, whether the satsumas are local, and what else is on the plate are the kitchen’s answers.

Offer it to the guest who wants something fresh before a rich holiday meal, or who is saving room for the turkey and the dessert. Satsumas are a Louisiana fall fruit, so the salad tastes of the season. Say: “It’s crisp endive with sweet satsuma, a cherry vinaigrette and roasted sunflower seeds: bright, light and very fall.” Suggest the rosé Crémant by the glass, whose red fruit meets the cherry.

Answer: A sweet, usually seedless mandarin that peels easily, first known in Japan and now the main citrus grown in south Louisiana. It is in season through the fall.

kept.a:
Sweet Potato Agnolotti brings two Southern harvests to an Italian pasta. Agnolotti are a filled pasta of Piedmont: where ravioli are two pieces of pasta sealed around a filling, agnolotti are one piece folded over it. The Agnolotti del Plin on our fall menu is the small pinched kind; this one is named for its sweet potato.

Louisiana has grown sweet potatoes for generations and sells them as yams, a marketing name since the 1930s; botanically a sweet potato is no yam at all. The Beauregard, an orange-fleshed variety released by the LSU AgCenter in 1987, became an industry standard.

The sheet adds candied pecans, brown butter and chèvre, French for goat and here goat cheese, tangy against the sweet filling. It prints no filling recipe, so learn at lineup what is in the pasta with the sweet potato and where the chèvre sits.

Sell it as Thanksgiving in a pasta: sweet potato and pecans, the flavors of the holiday table, in a tender Italian shape. Offer it to the guest who loves pasta, or who wants a rich, comforting start. Say: “It’s sweet potato agnolotti in brown butter with candied pecans and goat cheese: the holiday in a pasta.” With it, offer a glass of the Gainey Chardonnay, creamy enough for the brown butter.

Asked: What are agnolotti?

Answer: A filled pasta from Piedmont in northern Italy, made by folding one sheet of pasta over the filling. Ours is filled, as the name says, with sweet potato.

Asked: Is it sweet?

Answer: Gently. Sweet potato and candied pecans bring sweetness, and the brown butter and the tangy goat cheese balance it, so it eats as a savory pasta.

Asked: What is chèvre?

Answer: Goat cheese: chèvre is the French word for goat. Fresh chèvre is soft and tangy.

It is a Thanksgiving Day dish only. The sheet prints no filling recipe, so do not name what is mixed with the sweet potato until the kitchen tells you. Candied pecans, butter and cheese all raise questions: send every one to the kitchen before you answer. Do not confuse it with the Agnolotti del Plin of the fall menu. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.
